## Important Constraints

- **Forking requires a persisted parent session.** If the current session does not
  have a persisted session file, forked runs fail. Packaged `worker`, `oracle`,
  and `advisor` default to forked context, so use `context: "fresh"` explicitly
  when that is not available or not wanted.
- **Forked runs inherit parent history.** They are branched threads, not fresh
  filtered contexts. Use fresh context for adversarial reviewers unless the user explicitly asks for forked context.
- **Default subagent nesting depth is 2.** Deeper recursive delegation is blocked
  unless configured otherwise.
- **Attention signals are not lifecycle state.** `needs_attention` means no activity has been observed past the configured threshold. `paused` means the child turn was intentionally interrupted or is awaiting direction; it is not the same as `failed`.
- **Intercom asks are blocking.** A session can only maintain one pending outbound
  ask wait state at a time.
- **Keep conversational authority clear.** Advisory subagents should not silently
  become second decision-makers.
- **Respect the fixed authority policy.** `authorityPolicy` is a small `auto` / `confirm` / `forbid` map for supported operational actions. Worktree discard, destructive cleanup, and spawn-budget grants default to confirmation; stop, steer, and schedule creation remain automatic. Use `worktree.discard` with the durable `handoffPath`; confirm-required actions refuse safely without an interactive UI and retained paths include manual Git recovery commands.

Runtime config can change orchestration behavior. `intercomBridge.resultDelivery: false` disables only external acknowledged grouped-result delivery when native parent notifications own completion; supervisor asks/progress stay active, and enabled transport failures are still reported. `asyncByDefault` and `forceTopLevelAsync` affect whether launches detach; `waitTool` can make direct `subagent_wait()` calls return immediately while headless auto-drain remains active, and its effective value is propagated to child runtimes; `globalConcurrencyLimit` bounds concurrent fanout, while a positive `maxSubagentSpawnsPerSession` optionally caps cumulative launches (`0` or unset is unlimited). Status and doctor report the budget; static work preflights declared capacity; only the settled root interactive parent can use `grant-spawn-budget` after native confirmation, with total grants bounded by the original cap. Compaction does not reset usage or grants; `singleRunOutputBaseDir` and `worktreeBaseDir` route outputs and worktrees; `completionBatch` groups async notifications. `artifactDir` is `project` (default), `session`, or `temp` and chooses where subagent artifacts are stored. Set `asyncWidget: false` to hide the above-editor background-run widget when a companion footer or dashboard owns that space (fleet inspector remains available). Per-run `artifacts: false` disables artifact capture for that launch. Async status and result artifacts include `lifecycleArtifactVersion` and fields such as `workflowGraph`, `steps`, `results`, `totalTokens`, `totalCost`, `turnCount`, `toolCount`, and nested `children`. Child protocol failures expose a structured `protocolError`; `protocol_output_limit` means a child emitted a JSONL line above the 16 MiB live-parser cap. Prefer these artifacts and `status` views over scraping terminal output.

## Best Practices

### Prefer async orchestration

Launch every subagent asynchronously by default. Use `async: true` for scouts, researchers, workers, reviewers, validators, oracle checks, one-off delegates, and scripted workflows unless you intentionally need a foreground/blocking run. Launch all execution through `workflowScript`; use `return runs.run("main", { agent, task })` for one isolated child and `runs.all([...])` when two or more child lanes, monitors, or dependent steps should move together. The parent should keep moving: inspect code while scouts run, prepare validation while a worker implements, do a local diff pass while reviewers review, and synthesize or verify while a fix worker applies accepted feedback. Async is the default orchestration posture; foreground runs are the explicit opt-out.

### Use subagent_wait() to block until async runs finish

In an interactive chat, do not call `subagent_wait()` merely to wait after launching background work; return control to the user and Pi will wake the session on completion. Override that default when the current request is run-to-completion — for example, the user asked you to stay with the task and report results back this turn or a skill must finish in one turn. In a headless run, Pi auto-drains exact current-session work at `agent_end`; call `subagent_wait()` when this turn must receive results before it ends. In either case, `subagent_wait()` blocks the current turn until the next run completes or needs attention, keeps the turn alive for normal notification delivery, then returns.

- `subagent_wait()` — return when the next initially active async run or registered provider item finishes, or a subagent needs attention.
- `subagent_wait({ all: true })` — block until every async run and provider item active at call time finishes, or a subagent needs attention.
- `subagent_wait({ id: "..." })` — block on one async or remembered detached foreground run (id or prefix). Provider items are not selected through this parameter.
- `subagent_wait({ timeoutMs })` — cap the block; active work keeps running if it elapses.

Providers are discovered through the `pi-subagents/background-work` registry and must return stable item IDs with exact owning session IDs. Child agents receive no provider automatically: keep `subagent_wait` in the child `tools` allowlist and load provider extensions through `extensions` or `subagentOnlyExtensions`.

For non-interactive fleet orchestration, `subagent_wait()` can keep N workers in flight: launch N, wait for the next completion, react to the result, launch a replacement if needed, then wait again. Use `subagent_wait({ all: true })` only when you intentionally want to drain the fleet to zero. If the turn ends first, headless `agent_end` auto-drain still waits for exact current-session work. In an interactive session, return to the user instead of holding the turn open just to await completion.

If config or `PI_SUBAGENT_WAIT_TOOL_ENABLED` disables blocking behavior, direct `subagent_wait` calls return immediately. Headless `agent_end` auto-drain remains active as a lifecycle safeguard and surfaces provider, reconciliation, or timeout failures.

### Keep writes single-threaded by default

A strong pattern is one main decision-maker plus advisory/research/review/validation subagents around it. Use `oracle` for advice and `worker` for the actual write path. Parallelize reading, review, validation, and synthesis support, not normal writes, unless you deliberately isolate writers with worktrees. Across repositories, each repo/worktree still gets at most one writer, with explicit `cwd` and authority in the child prompt. A child that writes should report what changed, what was left undone, commands run with exit codes, validation evidence, surprises, and any decisions that need parent approval.

### Use fork for branched advisory or execution threads

Forked runs are useful when the child should reason in a separate thread while
still inheriting the parent’s accumulated context. They are especially useful for
`oracle`, which audits inherited decisions and drift. For adversarial code review,
prefer fresh-context reviewers that inspect the repo and diff directly unless the
user explicitly requests forked context.

### Prefer narrow tasks

Give subagents specific tasks rather than vague mandates.
`Review auth.ts for null-check gaps` works better than `Review everything`.

### Escalate decisions upward

If a subagent encounters an unapproved product, architecture, scope, merge, release, credential, or authority choice, it should use `contact_supervisor` and wait for the reply instead of deciding alone. Generic `intercom` is a fallback only when the bridge-provided supervisor tool is unavailable. External checks, receipts, and review bots provide evidence only; they do not grant authority.

### Intervene only on clear control signals

Use subagent control proactively when a delegated run emits `needs_attention`, or when a human asks you to regain control. Do not interrupt just because a child has briefly produced no output. Silence can be normal during long tool calls, test runs, or model reasoning.

### Name sessions meaningfully

Use `/name` so intercom targeting stays stable.

## Common Workflows

### Recon → Plan → Implement

```js
subagent({ workflowScript: `
  const context = await runs.run("recon", { agent: "scout", task: "Inspect the codebase and identify the implementation seam" });
  return (await runs.run("implement", { agent: "worker", task: "Implement from: " + context.output })).output;
` })
```

### Fable mode for complex work

Fable mode is the default orchestration posture for complex work. It is not a separate runtime mode; it is how the parent session uses `subagent`, `interview`, `subagent_wait`, acceptance contracts, artifacts, and fresh-context review when the work has real complexity. Use it for complex features, broad refactors, migrations, ambiguous goals, multi-system changes, expensive validation, user-visible behavior changes, or any request to plan/orchestrate end to end. Do not force it onto tiny one-shot delegation.

Run the work through seven gated phases:

1. **Understand** — use `scout` fanout for breadth, but the parent personally reads the load-bearing files and lets direct source reading decide disagreements. Gate: the parent can quote the exact code or behavior being changed and knows the repo's verification harness.
2. **Decide** — separate user-owned decisions from implementation judgments. Use `interview` for product, naming, cost, taste, risk, release, merge, or authority decisions; decide routine engineering details in the parent and state them. Gate: every user-owned decision needed for design is answered or recorded as a blocked follow-up.
3. **Design** — use read-only design/review children for parallel perspectives. Before parallel workstreams, write seam contracts: ownership boundaries, composition points, assumptions, and validation handoffs. Gate: one parent-synthesized plan and written seams for parallel work.
4. **Implement** — capture a baseline first, then launch one async `worker` as the sole writer for the active worktree unless isolated worktrees were intentionally requested. For cross-codebase work, launch separate async workers only when each has its own repo/worktree, explicit `cwd`, and non-overlapping authority. Break large work into serial milestones instead of concurrent writes. Gate: build/typecheck is green and every output or diff delta is characterized as intended or fixed.
5. **Verify** — climb the spend ladder: static checks, free end-to-end/dry-run, cheapest live probe, targeted changed-path live test, then full realistic run when warranted. Observe the artifact itself, not only exit codes or scores, and confirm the changed code actually executed. Gate: the highest necessary rung has directly observed evidence matching intent.
6. **Iterate** — when a gate or reviewer finds a defect, the parent names the failure class, searches for siblings, synthesizes fixes, and sends exactly one fix worker for accepted changes. For LLM judges, gates, or detectors, trigger on concrete findings rather than scores, record pass/violations/error verdicts, cache nondeterministic verdicts by input hash, budget enough output tokens, and sanitize judge text before reusing it downstream. Gate: the class is fixed or explicitly bounded, and recurrence detection exists when feasible.
7. **Ship** — run adversarial fresh-context review/validation outside the implementation path, disposition every finding, rerun affected gates, then have the parent inspect the final diff. Commit, push, comment, close, merge, release, or open PRs only inside user-approved boundaries for that repo. Gate: findings are dispositioned, gates re-pass, and the final summary names evidence, artifacts, residual risks, and output paths.

### Clarify → Plan → Implement → Review (self-orchestrated workflow)

For straightforward non-trivial work, this sequence is the lightweight version of the parent-owned loop. When the task is complex, use Fable mode above. In either case, factor in the packaged prompt workflows without literally invoking slash commands. Use the same patterns through tools and subagents.

Keep builtin agent defaults unless the user explicitly asks for a different model, thinking level, skills, output behavior, context mode, or other override. Do not add overrides just because you are orchestrating; the defaults encode the intended role behavior. In particular, packaged `worker`, `oracle`, and `advisor` default to forked context.

When the user approves launching a subagent to carry out a plan or workflow, treat that as approval to generate a proper role-specific meta prompt for that subagent. Include the approved plan path or summary, clarified requirements, non-goals, relevant context, role boundaries, files or areas to inspect, acceptance criteria, expected output, and validation expectations. Do not pass vague instructions like “implement the plan fully” or “review this” by themselves.

- `/gather-context-and-clarify` maps to: launch `scout` and, when needed, `researcher`; synthesize findings; then use `interview` to ask every clarification question needed for shared understanding.
- `/parallel-review` maps to: launch fresh-context `reviewer` agents with distinct review angles; synthesize the feedback before applying anything.
- `/review-loop` maps to: keep the parent in charge of worker → fresh reviewers → synthesized fix worker cycles until no fixes worth doing now remain, an unapproved decision appears, or the review-round cap is reached.
- `/parallel-research` maps to: combine local `scout` context with external `researcher` evidence when current docs, ecosystem behavior, or API details matter.
- `/parallel-cleanup` maps to: use review-only cleanup passes after implementation, especially for simplicity, verbosity, and redundant tests.

For feature work, use this sequence as scaffolding for parent-agent behavior:

```text
clarify → validation contract → scout → async worker → parallel async fresh-context reviewers/validators → async fix worker → follow-up review when warranted → parent review
```

The validation contract defines acceptance before code is written: expected behavior, acceptance checks, commands or user flows to exercise, and evidence the worker should return. Keep it lightweight for small tasks, but make it explicit enough that reviewers and validators are checking the intended outcome rather than the worker’s own assumptions.

For one host-run verification command, `gate: "npm test"` on the child is shorthand for verified acceptance with that command; it cannot be combined with `acceptance` and is rejected on retained resume items. Use the structured `acceptance` field when the run should carry an explicit acceptance contract. If omitted, subagents infer an effective policy from role, mode, and risk. Evidence levels end at `verified`: use `level: "checked"` for ordinary writer evidence and `level: "verified"` when the runtime should run explicit validation commands. Independent review is orthogonal; use `review: { required: true, agent: "reviewer" }` and orchestrate the reviewer separately. `review-required` means evidence passed but review is pending, while `reviewed` means a real independent result found no blockers. For reviewer/read-only calls, omit `acceptance`. Never explicitly request `level: "reviewed"`; that value remains recognized only so preflight can return an actionable correction. To disable gates, use `{ level: "none", reason: "..." }`; the bare string `"none"` is rejected, and `false` is accepted only as a deprecated shorthand. Child-reported command success is evidence, not runtime verification.

The first `worker` implements the approved plan. The parent continues with independent inspection or validation prep while it runs, not parallel edits to the same worktree. When the async worker completes, treat its handoff as the transition into review, not as final completion, unless the user explicitly asked for worker-only work, review-only output, or to stop after implementation. Parallel reviewers inspect the resulting diff from fresh context. Validators check behavior with the best available evidence: commands, tests, browser/CLI interaction, screenshots, logs, or manual reproduction notes. The final `worker` applies synthesized review fixes in forked context, then the parent looks over the final diff before completing. The parent may launch these steps as an initial async `workflowScript` when the workflow is already clear, or as follow-up workflowScript runs after each async completion. Initial workflows should pass `async: true` so the main chat is unblocked. Do not stop after parallel review unless the user explicitly asked for review-only output or the review surfaced a decision that needs approval first.

For complex work, risky changes, broad refactors, or many changed lines, increase review and validation fanout rather than trusting one reviewer. Use distinct angles such as correctness/regressions, tests/validation, simplicity/maintainability, security/privacy, performance, docs/API contracts, and user-flow behavior. When reviewers find non-trivial issues or the fix worker touches many lines, run another focused review round before final validation.

When review has already produced concrete findings across several independent areas, use staged fix orchestration: parallel read-only reviewers for each issue cluster, one sole writer worker for the active worktree, then parallel fresh-context validators. This is the safest way to handle a dirty worktree with many prior changes because it parallelizes judgment without parallelizing writes. Non-blocking suggestions may go into the writer prompt only if they are small, safe, and inside the approved scope; otherwise defer them explicitly.

For very large work, split into serial milestones instead of launching a swarm of writers. Each milestone gets one writer, a validation contract, fresh-context review/validation, a fix pass, and parent acceptance before the next milestone starts. Use parallel subagents inside a milestone for read-only context, research, review, and validation only.

Keep orchestration authority in the parent session. Child subagents should not launch more subagents, read this skill, or run their own orchestration loops unless the parent intentionally selected a fanout agent whose builtin `tools` includes `subagent`. Spawned subagents do not receive the `pi-subagents` skill, parent-only status/control/slash messages, or prior parent `subagent` tool-call/tool-result artifacts. Ordinary children also do not receive the `subagent` extension tool. Child context filtering strips old hidden orchestration-instruction messages when they appear in inherited history. Every child receives a boundary instruction: ordinary children are told the parent owns orchestration and they must not propose or run subagents; explicit fanout children are told to use `subagent` only for the assigned fanout work, with `maxSubagentDepth` still enforced. Implementation children must call real edit/write tools instead of printing pseudo tool calls. Pass children concrete role-specific work instead.

1. Clarify first. This is mandatory. Gather code context with `scout`, add `researcher` only when external evidence matters, then ask the user clarifying questions with `interview` until scope, acceptance criteria, constraints, and non-goals are clear.
2. Define the validation contract. State acceptance before implementation: expected behavior, checks to run, user flows to exercise, and evidence required in the worker handoff. For UI, CLI, integration, or workflow changes, include at least one validator angle that uses the product the way a user would rather than only reading code.
3. Plan when useful. For complex work, write a plan doc yourself and get approval before implementation. For simple work, confirm shared understanding and explicitly note why planning is skipped.
4. Implement with one writer. After approval, launch `worker` asynchronously with a proper meta prompt that includes clarified requirements, relevant context, plan path or summary, the validation contract, and output expectations. Packaged `worker` defaults to forked context; pass `context: "fresh"` only when you intentionally want a fresh child. While it runs, prepare validation or inspect adjacent code instead of editing the same worktree.
5. Require a useful worker handoff. Ask the worker to report changed files, what was implemented, what was left undone, commands run with exit codes, validation evidence, surprises or new risks, decisions made inside approved scope, and decisions needing parent approval.
6. Review after implementation. After the worker completes, launch parallel async fresh-context `reviewer` agents for correctness/regressions, tests/validation, and simplicity/maintainability. Add security, performance, docs/API, domain-specific, or user-flow validators for complex work, risky changes, broad refactors, or many changed lines. Use `output: false` unless review artifacts are explicitly needed.
7. Synthesize, then run the fix worker. Separate blockers, fixes worth doing now, optional improvements, and feedback to ignore/defer, then launch an async forked `worker` to apply fixes worth doing now when the workflow is implementation-authorized. If reviewers found scope/product/architecture choices that were not approved, ask the user first instead of applying them.
8. Review again when warranted. If the fix worker made substantial changes or addressed non-trivial findings, run another focused parallel review round before final validation.
9. Validate and complete. After the fix worker and any follow-up review return, inspect the final diff yourself, run or confirm focused validation, update docs/changelog when relevant, and summarize what changed and why.

Example implementation handoff after clarification and optional planning:

```typescript
subagent({
  workflowScript: `return runs.run("implementation", {
    agent: "worker",
    task: "Implement the approved feature.\n\nClarified requirements:\n- ...\n\nPlan: see ~/Documents/docs/...-plan.md\n\nValidation contract:\n- ...\n\nReturn a handoff with changed files, what was implemented, what was left undone, commands run with exit codes, validation evidence, surprises/new risks, and decisions needing parent approval.",
    acceptance: {
      level: "checked",
      evidence: ["changed-files", "tests-added", "commands-run", "residual-risks", "no-staged-files"]
    }
  })`,
  async: true
})
```

Example review pass after implementation:

```typescript
subagent({
  workflowScript: `
    const results = await runs.all([
      { key: "correctness", agent: "reviewer", task: "Review the current diff for correctness and regressions. Inspect changed files directly; do not rely on the worker's reasoning.", output: false },
      { key: "tests", agent: "reviewer", task: "Review the current diff for tests and validation quality against the validation contract. Inspect changed files directly.", output: false },
      { key: "simplicity", agent: "reviewer", task: "Review the current diff for simplicity and maintainability. Inspect changed files directly.", output: false }
    ]);
    return results.map(result => result.output);
  `,
  context: "fresh",
  async: true
})
```

Example fix worker after parallel reviews:

```typescript
subagent({
  workflowScript: `return runs.run("fix", {
    agent: "worker",
    task: "Apply the synthesized reviewer feedback below. Only apply fixes worth doing now; preserve user-approved scope; ask before unapproved product or architecture changes. Run focused validation and summarize what changed.\n\nReviewer synthesis:\n..."
  })`,
  async: true
})
```

### Review loop

Do not treat review as the final step for implementation work. Run reviewers and validators, synthesize their findings against user scope and the validation contract, then launch one `worker` for accepted fixes when implementation is authorized.

When an async implementation worker completes, treat the worker handoff as an intermediate state. The next parent action is review fanout, then synthesis, then a fix worker if reviewers found fixes worth doing now. This can be planned as an initial async `workflowScript` when the whole workflow is known, or continued as follow-up workflowScript runs when the parent only launched the first worker initially. Initial workflows should pass `async: true` so the main chat is unblocked.

For explicit review-loop requests, repeat worker → fresh-reviewer → synthesized-fix-worker cycles until reviewers find no blockers or fixes worth doing now, remaining feedback is optional or intentionally deferred, an unapproved product/scope/architecture decision needs the user, or the max review-round cap is reached. Default to 3 review rounds unless the user sets a different cap. For complex work, many changed lines, or any fix pass that materially changes the diff, run another focused review round before the parent’s final look; otherwise stop instead of chasing optional polish.

### Parallel non-conflicting analysis

```js
subagent({ workflowScript: `
  return await runs.all([
    { key: "frontend", agent: "scout", task: "Inspect the frontend" },
    { key: "backend", agent: "scout", task: "Inspect the backend" }
  ]);
` })
```

Use distinct keys, prompts, and output paths. Do not launch parallel writers into the same checkout.

## Error Handling

**"Unknown agent"**
```typescript
subagent({ action: "list" })
// Check available agents and chains, then confirm scope/precedence.
```

**Setup, discovery, or intercom confusion**
```typescript
subagent({ action: "doctor" })
// Check runtime paths, async support, discovery counts, current session, and intercom bridge state.
```

**"Max subagent depth exceeded"**
```typescript
// Flatten the workflow or raise maxSubagentDepth in config.
```

**"Session manager did not return a session file"**
```typescript
// Persist the current session before using context: "fork".
```

**Intercom "Already waiting for a reply"**
```typescript
// Resolve the current outbound ask before starting another one.
```

**Parallel output-path conflict**
```typescript
// Give each parallel task a distinct output path, or disable output for tasks that do not need it.
```

**Worktree launch fails**
```typescript
// Ensure the git working tree is clean and task cwd overrides match the shared cwd.
```

**Child fails before starting**
```typescript
// Inspect `subagent({ action: "status", id: "..." })`, artifact metadata/output logs, and run doctor. Extension loader errors usually appear in child output logs.
```

# Visual Review Rubric

Review every supplied wide-screen and narrow-screen render. Apply each relevant category and reject the interface for any critical failure.

## Product specificity

A passing interface visibly reflects the real product. It puts concrete evidence where the selected archetype requires it, while copy identifies a user, task, mechanism, result, or constraint.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `product-specificity.generic-interface` | Composition could represent an unrelated product | Replace generic regions with product-specific structure |
| `product-specificity.abstract-evidence` | Abstract decoration replaces product evidence | Show the interface, data, code, workflow, or technical diagram |
| `product-specificity.generic-copy` | Claims omit a product-specific task or mechanism | Name the user action and how the product supports it |

`product-specificity.logo-swap-test` is critical: a different logo and product noun make the interface suitable for an unrelated software company.

## Typography

A passing interface uses one UI family, reserves monospace for technical content, follows semantic roles, wraps headings naturally, and keeps body copy readable.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `typography.multiple-ui-fonts` | Several font personalities compete | Use the established UI family |
| `typography.decorative-heading` | Heading uses italics, gradient text, wide tracking, or manual breaks | Restore its semantic heading role |
| `typography.arbitrary-scale` | Type sizes do not form a coherent hierarchy | Map text to named roles |
| `typography.centered-long-copy` | Long prose is centered or too wide | Use a readable left-aligned measure |

## Composition

A passing composition follows its archetype. The primary task is obvious, reading order survives each viewport, and alignment or empty space clarifies groups.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `composition.archetype-gap` | Required region or state is absent | Add the missing functional region |
| `composition.competing-actions` | Several actions compete as primary | Establish one primary action |
| `composition.decorative-cards` | Cards fill space without useful grouping | Use plain layout, list, table, or dividers |
| `composition.mobile-order` | Narrow layout loses context or action priority | Reorder content around the primary task |
| `composition.spectacle-over-task` | Visual effect displaces product use | Center the composition on task evidence |

## Visual restraint and consistency

A passing interface gets hierarchy from scale and spacing, supported by weight, alignment, or grouping. Effects are functional and components share one token system.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `restraint.decorative-effects` | Gradients, glows, blobs, glass, or noise carry hierarchy | Restore semantic surfaces and typography |
| `restraint.decorative-imagery` | Generic imagery dominates product content | Replace it with concrete evidence |
| `restraint.pill-primary-control` | Primary control uses an oversized pill | Use the standard control radius |
| `restraint.multiple-systems` | Radius, shadow, border, icon, or color treatments conflict | Use the established token family |

## Content quality

Passing text uses concrete headings, controls with specific verbs and objects, explanations of mechanism or result, and qualified claims.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `content.generic-ai-language` | Copy relies on broad AI or transformation claims | Name the actual capability and result |
| `content.clever-over-clear` | Heading favors mood or wordplay over meaning | State the section purpose |
| `content.vague-action` | Control label is unspecific | Name the operation and object |
| `content.unqualified-claim` | Visible claim is absolute or unsupported | Bound or substantiate the claim |

## Accessibility

A passing render has readable contrast, visible keyboard focus, usable touch targets, logical order, clear control names, and motion that preserves access.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `accessibility.contrast` | Text or control lacks readable contrast | Use an approved accessible token pair |
| `accessibility.focus` | Supplied evidence shows no visible focus | Apply the system focus treatment |
| `accessibility.touch-target` | Control is too small or crowded for reliable touch | Increase its interactive area |
| `accessibility.label` | Control lacks a visible or inferable name | Add an associated label or accessible name |
| `accessibility.motion` | Motion hides content or ignores reduced-motion behavior | Preserve content and disable nonessential motion |

A task-critical control that cannot be perceived or operated is a critical failure.

## Responsive integrity

A passing interface keeps required content visible, adapts dense components deliberately, and does more than scale down the wide layout.

| Rule | Failure evidence | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| `responsive.clipping` | Required content clips, overlaps, or overflows | Reflow or constrain the affected region |
| `responsive.desktop-shrink` | Wide composition only shrinks | Define a narrow-layout reading order |
| `responsive.hidden-action` | Task-critical action disappears or loses context | Restore it near the relevant content |

A viewport that prevents the primary task is a critical failure.

## Result contract

Return this object:

```json
{
  "result": "pass",
  "critical_failures": [],
  "violations": [],
  "notes": []
}
```

Every finding names a rule, cites visible evidence, and identifies the affected viewport or state. Each non-critical violation includes a concrete correction. Set `result` to `fail` whenever either findings array contains an item.

Diagnosis:

- The mobile hamburger controls only the repository/session sidebar through [Layout.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/components/Layout.tsx:5) and [useMobileDrawer.ts](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/hooks/useMobileDrawer.ts:3).
- `Session` independently tracks a Boolean `workspacePanelOpen` state in [Session.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx:107).
- Mobile currently gets one generic “Workspace” button. It opens a full-screen overlay containing the entire inspector ([Session.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx:540), [Session.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx:674)).
- The explorer and terminal already exist in [WorkspaceInspector.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/components/WorkspaceInspector.tsx:651), but are vertically stacked. The terminal is a fixed-height bottom pane rather than a separately navigable mobile destination ([WorkspaceInspector.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/components/WorkspaceInspector.tsx:686), [WorkspaceInspector.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/components/WorkspaceInspector.tsx:743)).
- Desktop behavior starts at 1024px and should remain unchanged: chat plus resizable inspector ([Session.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx:656)).
- `index.css` supplies iOS safe-area padding and 16px form controls but no workspace-specific responsive behavior ([index.css](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/index.css:5)).
- The provided screenshot was not mounted, so this assessment uses its description and the repository implementation.

Recommended responsive state flow:

```text
Mobile session
  Files button ───→ full-screen workspace overlay in Files mode
  Terminal button → full-screen workspace overlay in Terminal mode
                         ↕ switch modes within overlay
                       Close → return to chat

Desktop session
  unchanged split view: chat | resizer | combined inspector
```

Replace the Boolean mobile state with a discriminated state such as `null | "files" | "terminal"`. Give `WorkspaceInspector` a presentation/view prop so mobile displays one tool at a time while its default desktop presentation retains the existing stacked explorer and terminal. Explicit “Files” and “Terminal” controls are preferable to the ambiguous “Workspace” label.

TDD Guard test order:

1. Extend [Session.test.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/pages/__tests__/Session.test.tsx:184) first:

   - Clicking each opens the overlay in the requested mode.
   - Switching modes and closing returns to chat.
   - Controls are absent when `workspace_id` is null.
   - Mock `WorkspaceInspector` so these remain focused session-state tests.

2. Extend [WorkspaceInspector.test.tsx](/workspace/yinshi/frontend/src/components/__tests__/WorkspaceInspector.test.tsx:149):
   - Files mode exposes the explorer and does not mount/open the terminal.
   - Terminal mode opens and fits the terminal without showing the file browser.
   - Default/split mode preserves the current desktop structure and terminal behavior.

3. Add a small mobile Playwright case near `navigation.spec.ts`:
   - Use an iPhone-sized viewport.
   - Open Files, return to chat, open Terminal, and confirm terminal UI visibility.
   - Confirm the global hamburger still controls only the sidebar.

No changes appear necessary in `Sidebar`, `Layout`, or `useMobileDrawer`; combining their state with session tools would couple unrelated navigation.

name: surf
description: Control Chrome through the surf CLI for browser testing, screenshots, form filling, page inspection, network and CPU emulation, DevTools data, and AI sites that use your logged-in Chrome session.
---

# Surf Browser Automation

`surf` gives agents a real Chrome session. Use it when shell-only checks cannot prove browser behavior: page state, clicks, forms, screenshots, console output, network requests, viewport changes, or AI sites that require your logged-in Chrome profile.

When command syntax is uncertain, ask the CLI first.

```bash
surf --help
surf <group>
surf --help-full
surf --find <term>
surf --help-topic <topic>
```

## First pass on a page

```bash
surf navigate "https://example.com"
surf page.read
surf page.read --compact
surf page.state
surf screenshot --output /tmp/shot.png
```

Read the page before clicking. Refs from `page.read` usually survive markup churn better than CSS selectors. Semantic locators work well when the intent is visible in the UI.

```bash
surf click --ref e1
surf locate.role button --name "Submit" --action click
surf locate.label "Email" --action fill --value "test@example.com"
surf locate.text "Accept" --exact --action click
```

## Browser targets

```bash
surf tab.list
surf tab.new "https://google.com"
surf tab.switch 12345
surf tab.name myapp
surf tab.switch myapp
surf tab.close 12345

surf window.list --tabs
surf window.new "https://example.com"
surf --window-id 123 page.read
surf window.focus 12345
surf window.resize --id 123 --width 1920 --height 1080
```

Use a separate window when agent work should not disturb your normal tabs.

## Read, act, wait

```bash
surf page.text
surf page.read --ref e5
surf element.styles e5
surf element.styles ".card"

surf click --x 100 --y 200
surf click --ref e5
surf type --text "hello"
surf type --text "hello" --selector "#input" --method js
surf key Enter
surf key "cmd+a"
surf hover --ref e5
surf drag --from-x 100 --from-y 100 --to-x 200 --to-y 200

surf scroll.bottom
surf scroll.to --ref e5
surf scroll.by --y 200
surf scroll.info

surf wait 2
surf wait.element ".loaded"
surf wait.network
surf wait.url "/success"
surf wait.dom --stable 100
surf wait.load
```

Use `--method js` when CDP typing fails in rich text editors.

## Forms and embedded contexts

```bash
surf form.fill --data '[{"ref":"e1","value":"John"},{"ref":"e2","value":"john@example.com"}]'
surf select e5 "Option A"
surf select e5 --by label "Display Text"
surf upload --ref e5 --files "/path/to/file.txt"

surf frame.list
surf frame.switch "FRAME_ID"
surf frame.main
surf frame.js --id "FRAME_ID" --code "return document.title"

surf dialog.info
surf dialog.accept
surf dialog.accept --text "response"
surf dialog.dismiss
```

Switch into an iframe before reading or acting on elements inside it.

## Evidence and diagnostics

```bash
surf screenshot
surf screenshot --output /tmp/shot.png
surf screenshot --selector ".card"
surf screenshot --full-page

surf console
surf console --stream --level error
surf network
surf network --stream
surf network.get --id "req-123"
surf network.body --id "req-123"
surf network.curl --id "req-123"
surf network.export

surf perf.metrics
surf perf.start
surf perf.stop
surf wait.element ".missing" --auto-capture --timeout 2000
```

`--auto-capture` saves the screenshot and console snapshot needed to debug failed waits.

## Emulation and stored browser state

```bash
surf emulate.network slow-3g
surf emulate.network reset
surf emulate.cpu 4
surf emulate.cpu 1
surf emulate.device "iPhone 14"
surf emulate.device --list
surf emulate.viewport --width 1280 --height 720
surf emulate.touch --enable
surf emulate.geo --lat 37.7749 --lon -122.4194
surf emulate.geo --clear

surf zoom
surf zoom 1.5
surf zoom 1
surf cookie.list
surf cookie.get --name "token"
surf cookie.clear
surf history --query "github" --max 20
surf bookmarks --query "docs"
surf bookmark.add --url "https://..." --title "My Bookmark"
```

After tests, restore network throttling; clear device settings; remove any location override; reset zoom.

## AI sites through Chrome

These commands rely on your logged-in Chrome profile. No API key is involved.

```bash
surf chatgpt "explain this code"
surf chatgpt "review" --with-page --model gpt-4o
surf chatgpt "analyze" --file document.pdf

surf gemini "summarize" --with-page
surf gemini "analyze" --file data.csv
surf gemini "a robot surfing" --generate-image /tmp/robot.png
surf gemini "hello" --model gemini-2.5-flash

surf perplexity "latest news" --model sonar
surf perplexity "deep dive" --mode research

surf grok "find viral AI posts" --deep-search
surf grok --validate
surf grok --validate --save-models

surf aistudio "redteam this" --with-page
surf aistudio "quick answer" --model gemini-3-flash-preview
surf aistudio.build "build a portfolio site" --output ./out
```

On failure, check login state, validate the UI, increase timeout for thinking models, then retry with a model name from validation output.

## Multi-step scripts

`surf do` runs a browser flow as one command, with automatic waits after page loads, clicks, keys, form fills, and tab switches.

```bash
surf do 'go "https://example.com" | click e5 | screenshot'
surf do 'go "https://example.com/login" | type "user@example.com" --selector "#email" | type "pass" --selector "#password" | click --selector "button[type=submit]"'
surf do 'go "https://example.test" | page.read' --dry-run
```

Named workflows live in `~/.surf/workflows/` or `./.surf/workflows/`.

```bash
surf workflow.list
surf workflow.info my-workflow
surf do my-workflow --email "user@example.com" --password "secret"
surf workflow.validate workflow.json
```

Workflow files can store step output, loop a fixed number of times, iterate over data, or stop when a condition passes.

```json
{
  "steps": [
    { "tool": "js", "args": { "code": "return [1,2,3]" }, "as": "items" },
    { "repeat": 5, "steps": [{ "tool": "click", "args": { "ref": "e5" } }] },
    { "each": "%{items}", "as": "item", "steps": [
      { "tool": "js", "args": { "code": "console.log('%{item}');" } }
    ]}
  ]
}
```

```bash
surf do my-workflow --file workflow.json --json
surf do 'go "https://example.org" | screenshot' --on-error stop --step-delay 100
surf do 'go "https://example.net" | wait.load' --no-auto-wait
```

## Common options

```bash
--tab-id <id>
--window-id <id>
--json
--auto-capture
--timeout <ms>
```

## Socket API

Send a JSON tool request to the Unix socket when another process needs direct access.

```bash
echo '{"type":"tool_request","method":"execute_tool","params":{"tool":"tab.list","args":{}},"id":"1"}' | nc -U /tmp/surf.sock
```

---
name: software-design
description: Applies principles from "A Philosophy of Software Design" to architecture, module and API boundaries, and consequential refactors. Use for architecture planning, module or API design, design review, or diagnosing shallow modules, information leakage, and pass-through layers.
---

# Software Design

Apply these principles when architecture or abstraction quality is a material part of the task.

## Two Modes

### Writing New Code

Apply these principles in order of impact.

#### Think strategically

Invest in design instead of stopping when the code first works. Produce a clean design that works, and spend 10–20% of the effort on design improvements.

#### Create deep modules

Each module should provide powerful functionality behind a simple interface. A few deep methods beat many shallow ones. Ask whether the interface is simpler than the implementation.

#### Hide information

Each module should encapsulate design decisions that remain invisible through its interface. If one decision appears in several modules, reorganize the code until that decision has one home.

#### Make interfaces general-purpose

Design an interface broad enough to support current uses while keeping its functionality focused. Ask for the simplest interface that covers every current need.

#### Give each layer a different abstraction

Adjacent layers should operate at different abstraction levels. Remove pass-through methods that delegate with the same signature.

#### Pull complexity downwards

Handle complexity inside the module instead of pushing it to callers. A simple interface matters more than a simple implementation.

#### Define errors out of existence

Redefine APIs so avoidable error conditions cannot arise. Mask low-level exceptions and consolidate their handling. Reserve crashes for unrecoverable failures.

#### Design it twice

Consider at least two radically different approaches before committing. Compare their strengths and costs. Apply this comparison to interfaces and implementations, then consider the broader system decomposition.

#### Name precisely

Names should create a clear mental image of an entity's purpose. Avoid vague choices such as `data`, `result`, `info`, or `tmp`. Name booleans with predicates such as `isConnected` instead of a state label such as `status`.

#### Be consistent

Use the same name for the same purpose everywhere. Reuse established coding patterns and conventions. Consistency reduces the reader's cognitive work.

#### Make code obvious

Code is obvious when a reader's first guess about its behaviour is correct. Choose precise names and follow established patterns. Use whitespace to expose structure, and comment only where the code cannot explain itself.

#### Write comments first

Write interface comments before implementation. A method that needs a long descriptive comment has a complex interface and should be redesigned. Comments should preserve information that code cannot represent.

### Reviewing Existing Code

Scan for these red flags in the listed order.

#### Shallow modules

Look for interfaces as complex as their implementations, many trivial methods, or classes with little functionality.

#### Information leakage

Find design decisions repeated across modules. A change to one detail should not require coordinated edits across several classes.

#### Temporal decomposition

Check for code organized around operation order instead of information hiding, such as separate read and write classes for one format.

#### Pass-through methods

Flag methods that only call another method with the same signature, especially when delegation accounts for half or more of a class's methods.

#### Overexposure

A common operation should not force callers to understand rare features. Default information that callers should not have to provide.

#### Conjoined methods

Flag a method when understanding it requires reading another method's implementation.

#### Repetition

Find non-trivial code patterns duplicated in several places.

#### Vague or hard-to-pick names

Flag names broad enough to describe many entities. Difficulty finding a precise name often means the entity has too many responsibilities.

#### Comment problems

Find comments that restate the code or expose implementation details in interface documentation. Long, complicated descriptions may reveal a poor abstraction.

#### Special-general mixture

Keep specialized use-case code out of a general-purpose mechanism.

#### Nonobvious code

Flag behaviour that a quick reading cannot reveal, including surprising side effects.

#### Too many exceptions

# Git Workflow

1. Inspect the worktree and preserve unrelated user changes. Stage only files that belong to the completed task.
2. Write a commit message that explains what changed and why, so future readers do not need to reconstruct the decision from the diff.
3. Pull the remote branch with rebase before pushing. Continue without asking for routine confirmation; stop for user input if a merge conflict requires a decision.
4. Push to the correct branch, usually `main` or `master`.

The workflow is complete when the task's commit exists on the remote branch, or when a merge conflict has been reported with the conflicting paths and required decision.

# Red Flags Checklist

Use this checklist during code review or when writing new code. Each red flag indicates a likely design problem.

## Module Structure

### Shallow Module
- [ ] The interface for a class or method is not much simpler than its implementation.
- [ ] A method's body is trivially short (one or two lines) but its signature and documentation are comparable in size.
- [ ] The class has many methods, each doing very little.

### Classitis
- [ ] The system has many small classes, each with minimal functionality.
- [ ] Using a feature requires creating or coordinating multiple objects that could be one.
- [ ] The number of interfaces grows faster than the total functionality.

## Information Problems

### Information Leakage
- [ ] The same design decision (file format, protocol detail, data representation) is reflected in multiple modules.
- [ ] Changing one implementation detail requires coordinated changes across several classes.
- [ ] Two classes both understand the same internal format even though neither exposes it in its interface.

### Temporal Decomposition
- [ ] Code structure mirrors the time order of operations rather than grouping by knowledge.
- [ ] Separate classes for "read" and "write" operations on the same format, or "parse" and "process" phases that share knowledge.

### Overexposure
- [ ] Using a commonly needed feature forces callers to learn about rarely used features.
- [ ] The API requires callers to provide information that could be defaulted or computed automatically.
- [ ] Creating a simple object requires multiple steps involving auxiliary objects (e.g., Java's FileInputStream + BufferedInputStream + ObjectInputStream).

## Method Problems

### Pass-Through Method
- [ ] A method does almost nothing except invoke another method with the same or similar signature.
- [ ] 50% or more of a class's methods simply delegate to another class.

### Conjoined Methods
- [ ] Understanding one method requires understanding the implementation of another.
- [ ] Two physically separated pieces of code can only be understood together.

### Repetition
- [ ] The same non-trivial code pattern appears in multiple places.
- [ ] A bug fix in one location needs to be replicated in several others.

## Naming and Clarity

### Vague Name
- [ ] A variable or method name is broad enough to refer to many different things (e.g., `data`, `result`, `info`, `tmp`, `count` without context).
- [ ] A boolean variable's name does not clearly convey what true/false means (e.g., `status` instead of `isConnected`).

### Hard to Pick Name
- [ ] It is difficult to find a precise, intuitive name for a variable or method.
- [ ] The entity might be trying to represent multiple things at once.

## Documentation Problems

### Comment Repeats Code
- [ ] The comment restates what the code already says in the same words.
- [ ] The comment could be written by someone who never saw any code except the line next to the comment.

### Implementation Documentation Contaminates Interface
- [ ] An interface comment (class or method) describes implementation details not needed by users.
- [ ] Internal data structure names, algorithm details, or configuration constants appear in public documentation.

### Hard to Describe
- [ ] A complete description of a method or variable requires a long, complicated comment.
- [ ] This suggests the abstraction may not be clean.

## Design Problems

### Special-General Mixture
- [ ] A general-purpose mechanism also contains code specialized for a particular use case.
- [ ] Future changes to the use case will likely require changes to the underlying mechanism.

### Nonobvious Code
- [ ] The behavior or meaning of code cannot be understood with a quick reading.
- [ ] The code does something surprising relative to reader expectations (e.g., a constructor that spawns threads, a method with hidden side effects).

## Exception Handling

### Too Many Exceptions
- [ ] The class throws exceptions for conditions the caller cannot reasonably handle.
- [ ] Each method call is wrapped in its own try-catch block.
- [ ] Error handling code is longer than normal-case code.

### Missing Error Elimination
- [ ] An API defines error conditions that could be eliminated by slightly redefining the operation's semantics.
- [ ] Special cases that could be handled by the normal code path are instead checked explicitly.

# Orchestration

Pi uses a Sol parent to plan work and route bounded tasks. The parent validates changes and completes the final review.

## Role map

| Role | Model | Responsibility | Write access |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parent | `openai-codex/gpt-5.6-sol` | Plans and routes work. Validates changes and reviews them. | Yes |
| `scout` | `local-pilocal/qwen36-35b-a3b-iq4xs-mtp3-turbo3` | Fast repository reconnaissance | No |
| `test-writer` | `local-pilocal/qwen36-35b-a3b-iq4xs-mtp3-turbo3` | One behavior-facing failing test | Tests only |
| `worker` | `openai-codex/gpt-5.6-luna` | Standard implementation tasks | Yes |
| `worker-advanced` | `z-ai/glm-5.3` | Advanced implementation tasks | Yes |
| `reviewer` | `local-pilocal/qwen36-35b-a3b-iq4xs-mtp3-turbo3` | Mechanical advisory review | No |

The parent runs with thinking level `max`. Child definitions pin their models so routing does not depend on parent inheritance.

## Automatic routing

Normal coding prompts use this policy without `/orchestra`.

| Class | Route | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct | Sol parent | Trivial corrections where delegation costs more than implementation |
| Standard | `worker` | Default delegated work with architecture already decided |
| Advanced | `worker-advanced` | Work with a specific implementation-level correctness risk |

Standard work goes to Luna High through `worker`. Large file counts or important features do not make work advanced when implementation is mechanical.

Advanced work goes to GLM-5.3 Max through `worker-advanced`. Qualifying risks include concurrency, cancellation, ownership, retry behavior, recovery, durable state, transaction ordering, migrations, credential lifecycle, authorization, security boundaries, or irreversible external effects.

Default to Standard when classification is ambiguous. Choose Advanced only after naming the specific advanced risk. Prefer Advanced for security boundary changes, destructive recovery, credential lifecycle changes, and irreversible safeguards.

The parent may call `scout` when repository mapping will reduce uncertainty. It may call `test-writer` after expected behavior is defined. It may call `reviewer` for optional mechanical pre-review when a meaningful non-trivial diff makes a cheap mechanical pass useful. Skip reviewer for trivial edits, small obvious patches, copy or style-only changes, or changes Sol can inspect cheaply. These Qwen roles can be selected automatically.

Reviewer remains read-only and advisory. It cannot edit, commit, push, launch children, or alter repository state. The test writer must finish before either implementation worker starts. Reviewer findings never narrow Sol review.

No hard file-count or line-count threshold determines reviewer usage. Sol decides based on the diff nature. Sol final review remains mandatory after delegated implementation.

## Writer ordering

Only one writer may operate in the active checkout at a time. This rule covers `test-writer`, `worker`, correction workers, and any future advanced worker.

Read-only scouts and reviewers may run independently when their tasks do not depend on pending writes. Reviewer output remains advisory. The Sol parent accepts or rejects each finding.

## Parent duties

The Sol parent reads repository instructions and inspects relevant files. It defines expected behavior before creating bounded task packets.

The parent chooses routing before delegation. It inspects every child result and changed file. Focused checks run before broader relevant checks.

The parent evaluates reviewer findings. Resume the original child for accepted corrections when practical. Otherwise dispatch the same implementation role. Escalate only when review exposes a concrete routing error.

Delegated tasks use fresh child context by default. Each task packet states context references and expected behavior. It also states critical invariants, required checks, and escalation conditions.

The parent then independently reviews the original task, approved plan, critical invariants, actual final diff, and relevant checks. It completes the authoritative final review even when reviewer reports no findings.

For concurrency, recovery, persistence, authorization, credential lifecycle, security, protocols, cryptography, or irreversible actions, Sol performs substantive correctness review. Reviewer may catch mechanical defects but cannot certify those semantics.

`/orchestra` guarantees the complete context-engineered workflow. Normal prompts may skip unnecessary utility agents. The command does not grant commit, push, release, or unrelated cleanup authority.

## Installation

Install supported orchestration files and the PiLocal launcher:

```bash
npm run install:orchestra
```

The installer removes only named retired orchestration files and the retired local subagent extension. It preserves unrelated agents and prompts. Other extensions remain unchanged.

Z.ai remains a machine-local Pi provider. Keep its credentials and endpoint outside this repository.

## Validation

Run repository checks with Node 24 or newer:

```bash
npm run test:orchestra
node --test scripts/extension-layout.test.ts
bash -n scripts/pilocal
npm run lint:prose
```

Strict `subagents.modelScope` allows the exact Qwen model and Luna model. It also allows GLM-5.3. Per-role overrides enforce each assignment.

# Software Design Review: `958a612`

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Date | 2026-08-12 |
| Commit | `958a612030b0236c0e4667f49c02ce1ac2f2e92b` |
| Comparison | First parent through `958a612` |
| Scope | Managed backup lifecycle and supporting APIs |
| Lens | Principles from *A Philosophy of Software Design* |
| Outcome | All confirmed material defects were fixed |

## Summary

The commit introduced durable managed backup and restore. Its structure is sound. The catalog owns persistent state. The manager coordinates provider work. The relay controls live transport.

The review found three concrete defects at recovery boundaries. Each correction moved recovery knowledge into its owning module. No broad restructuring was needed.

## Confirmed findings and corrections

### High: Create operations omitted durable source identity

`backend/src/yinshi/services/managed_backups.py` created backup operations without `source_runner_id` or `source_sprite_id`. Relay recovery therefore could not reconstruct a maintenance fence after process restart.

Correction: `start_managed_backup_creation()` now copies both identities from the exact ready runtime into the operation transaction. A database-backed relay restart test confirms that a new broker rejects transfers and sends the exact job-bound quiesce frame.

Design effect: recovery no longer depends on live manager memory. The catalog now contains the identity required to interpret its own durable operation.

### High: Failed restore cleanup retained unusable candidate identity

`backend/src/yinshi/services/managed_backup_manager.py` deleted a failed candidate but retained its runner and Sprite IDs. A later claim could attempt to reuse a deleted candidate.

Correction: `clear_managed_backup_candidate()` clears the exact leased candidate and returns the restore phase to `claimed`. The manager calls it only after provider deletion succeeds. If deletion fails, durable identity remains available for another cleanup attempt.

Design effect: provider deletion and catalog transition now have one clear ordering rule. The retry path does not need to infer whether a named candidate still exists.

### Medium: Durable catalog conflicts escaped as HTTP 500 responses

`backend/src/yinshi/api/managed_runtime.py` handled `ValueError` but not `ManagedBackupConflictError`. Expected concurrent-operation conflicts could reach the generic server-error path.

Correction: all managed backup mutation routes map both state exceptions to the existing safe HTTP 409 response. Provider text remains private.

Design effect: the API masks a lower-level persistence exception behind one stable client contract.

## Additional recovery correction

Recovered relay maintenance initially blocked transfers but treated quiescence as already acknowledged. Coordination could resume before the reconnected runner confirmed that services and writers had stopped.

`RunnerRelayBroker` now creates a pending acknowledgment future when it reconstructs maintenance from the catalog. Same-job `quiesce_runner()` calls wait for the exact runner acknowledgment. Duplicate reconnect acknowledgments are safe. Failed catalog lookups do not publish dead connections. The relay sends `welcome` before recovered maintenance control.

The migration fills missing source identities for matching running operations. This lets relay fencing survive upgrades from the earlier schema.

## Design assessment

### Module depth

`ManagedBackupManager` presents a small queue-and-reconcile interface. It hides provider coordination, lease handling, encrypted jobs, and crash recovery.

### Information hiding

The catalog owns durable operation state and lease checks. The relay reads only the operation needed to restore its fence. API routes hide storage metadata.

### Error handling

Expected state conflicts now have one public representation. Candidate deletion is idempotent because a missing Sprite counts as deleted. Unexpected provider failures leave enough durable state for retry.

### Remaining risks

Public managed launch must remain disabled. Uncertain immutable uploads still require durable exact-version reconciliation. Live disaster-recovery drills still need independent versioned object storage. Sprite storage-encryption verification also remains incomplete.

These risks are outside the three reviewed defects. They remain launch gates rather than regressions introduced by these corrections.

## Validation

Backend validation passed 1,238 tests after the final reviewer corrections. Black and isort checks passed. Flake8 and strict mypy also passed.

Frontend Vitest passed. Type checking and the production build passed. Sidecar Node tests passed. Desktop tests passed with type checking and build checks.

`pip-audit` reported no known vulnerabilities. `git diff --check` passed.

# Software Design Review: `840b021`

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Date | 2026-08-25 |
| Commit | `840b02189f8eb9be6db859853d3f03ad4cf1e3e1` |
| Comparison | Parent commit through `840b021` |
| Scope | Mobile Files and Terminal access in session workspaces |
| Lens | Principles from *A Philosophy of Software Design* |
| Status | Correction pending |

## Summary

The commit makes Files and Terminal available as separate mobile workspace views. It keeps the combined desktop inspector and prevents file activity when only the terminal is shown.

The review found four material design issues. Two affect production vocabulary and ownership. One repeats a lifecycle rule. One makes browser checks and captures less trustworthy. No other material design findings remain within the commit scope.

## Findings

### Medium: Mobile workspace state has a Boolean-style name

`frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx` names the state `workspacePanelOpen`, but the value stores `"files"`, `"terminal"`, or `null`.

This name hides the state meaning. A reader can mistake it for a Boolean and add incorrect conditions.

Required correction: rename the state to `activeMobileWorkspaceView` and rename its setter to match.

### Medium: Workspace tool vocabulary is repeated across modules and controls

`frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx` declares its own tool union and repeats Files and Terminal button definitions in the session header and mobile overlay. `frontend/src/components/WorkspaceInspector.tsx` declares the related inspector view union separately.

Adding or renaming a tool therefore requires coordinated edits in several locations. The tool contract and display labels lack one owner.

Required correction: export a narrow workspace tool type and one descriptor list from the inspector module. Derive the broader inspector view type from that tool type. Render both mobile control groups from the shared descriptors.

### Low: File activity gating repeats the same view rule

`frontend/src/components/WorkspaceInspector.tsx` repeats `!active || view === "terminal"` in file refresh and polling paths.

A later view change could update one path but miss another. The lifecycle rule should have one precise predicate.

Required correction: derive one file-activity predicate and reuse it in refresh callbacks and polling lifecycle checks.

### Low: Browser viewport helper and capture timing hide intent

`frontend/e2e/navigation.spec.ts` passes an unused name to `assertInViewport`, hard-codes one viewport size, and captures the initial session before readiness checks.

The helper cannot safely validate another viewport. The early capture can show an empty page even when the test later passes.

Required correction: remove the unused argument, read the current viewport dimensions, and capture the initial session after all header controls are ready.

## Preserved requirements

Corrections must preserve these behaviors:

- Files and Terminal remain directly available on mobile.
- All mobile header controls fit within a 390 by 844 viewport.
- Files mode does not connect the terminal.
- Terminal mode does not poll workspace files.
- Users can switch tools and return to chat.
- Safe-area padding remains active on the mobile overlay.
- Desktop keeps one combined inspector across responsive transitions.

## Required validation

- Focused Session and WorkspaceInspector unit tests
- Complete frontend unit tests
- Navigation Playwright tests
- TypeScript checking
- Production build
- Git whitespace check

## Final assessment

Correction work has not started. This document will be updated with the exact changes and final validation results after the orchestration workflow completes.

# Software Design Review: `840b021`

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Date | 2026-08-25 |
| Commit | `840b02189f8eb9be6db859853d3f03ad4cf1e3e1` |
| Comparison | Parent commit through `840b021` |
| Scope | Mobile Files and Terminal access in session workspaces |
| Lens | Principles from *A Philosophy of Software Design* |
| Status | Complete |

## Summary

The commit makes Files and Terminal available as separate mobile workspace views. It keeps the combined desktop inspector and prevents file activity when only the terminal is shown.

The review found four material design issues. Two affect production vocabulary and ownership. One repeats a lifecycle rule. One makes browser checks and captures less trustworthy. No other material design findings remain within the commit scope.

## Findings

### Medium: Mobile workspace state has a Boolean-style name

`frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx` names the state `workspacePanelOpen`, but the value stores `"files"`, `"terminal"`, or `null`.

This name hides the state meaning. A reader can mistake it for a Boolean and add incorrect conditions.

Required correction: rename the state to `activeMobileWorkspaceView` and rename its setter to match.

### Medium: Workspace tool vocabulary is repeated across modules and controls

`frontend/src/pages/Session.tsx` declares its own tool union and repeats Files and Terminal button definitions in the session header and mobile overlay. `frontend/src/components/WorkspaceInspector.tsx` declares the related inspector view union separately.

Adding or renaming a tool therefore requires coordinated edits in several locations. The tool contract and display labels lack one owner.

Required correction: export a narrow workspace tool type and one descriptor list from the inspector module. Derive the broader inspector view type from that tool type. Render both mobile control groups from the shared descriptors.

### Low: File activity gating repeats the same view rule

`frontend/src/components/WorkspaceInspector.tsx` repeats `!active || view === "terminal"` in file refresh and polling paths.

A later view change could update one path but miss another. The lifecycle rule should have one precise predicate.

Required correction: derive one file-activity predicate and reuse it in refresh callbacks and polling lifecycle checks.

### Low: Browser viewport helper and capture timing hide intent

`frontend/e2e/navigation.spec.ts` passes an unused name to `assertInViewport`, hard-codes one viewport size, and captures the initial session before readiness checks.

The helper cannot safely validate another viewport. The early capture can show an empty page even when the test later passes.

Required correction: remove the unused argument, read the current viewport dimensions, and capture the initial session after all header controls are ready.

## Preserved requirements

Corrections must preserve these behaviors:

- Files and Terminal remain directly available on mobile.
- All mobile header controls fit within a 390 by 844 viewport.
- Files mode does not connect the terminal.
- Terminal mode does not poll workspace files.
- Users can switch tools and return to chat.
- Safe-area padding remains active on the mobile overlay.
- Desktop keeps one combined inspector across responsive transitions.

## Corrections

### Precise mobile state

`Session` now uses `activeMobileWorkspaceView` and `setActiveMobileWorkspaceView`. The state type is `WorkspaceTool | null`, so its name and valid values describe the same concept.

### One workspace tool vocabulary

`WorkspaceInspector` now exports one readonly descriptor tuple. `WorkspaceTool` derives from its key values. Both mobile control groups render from the same descriptors, so tool keys and labels have one production owner.

### One file-activity rule

`WorkspaceInspector` now derives `hasFileActivity` once. Initial refresh, changed-file refresh, focus refresh, and polling reuse that predicate. Terminal-only mode remains free from file requests.

### Accurate browser checks and captures

The Playwright viewport helper now reads the active viewport dimensions and has no unused parameter. The initial session capture runs after Files, Terminal, Model, and Thinking controls are visible and within bounds.

## Validation

- Focused Session and WorkspaceInspector unit tests passed: 39 tests.
- Complete frontend unit tests passed: 376 tests across 43 files.
- Navigation Playwright tests passed: 4 tests.
- TypeScript checking passed.
- Production build passed.
- Git whitespace check passed.

The test run emitted existing local-storage, Browserslist, and Authlib warnings. Intentional chunk-error tests also logged their expected exceptions. None caused a test or build failure.

## Final assessment

All four findings are corrected. Advisory review found no remaining blocker. Parent review found and corrected one final duplication between the tool type and descriptor list. No material software-design finding remains within the reviewed scope.

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: backend
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
      - uses: actions/setup-python@ece7cb06caefa5fff74198d8649806c4678c61a1 # v6.3.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: backend/requirements/*.txt
      - run: python -m pip install --upgrade pip==26.1.2
      - run: python -m pip install -r requirements/dev.txt pip-audit==2.10.1
      - run: python -m pip install --no-deps -e .
      - run: pytest -q
      - run: black --check src tests
      - run: isort --check-only src tests
      - run: flake8 src tests
      - run: mypy src
      - run: pip-audit

  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: frontend
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: frontend/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm exec vitest run
      - run: npm run typecheck
      - run: npm run build
      - run: npm audit

  desktop:
    runs-on: macos-15
    timeout-minutes: 45
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
      - uses: actions/setup-python@ece7cb06caefa5fff74198d8649806c4678c61a1 # v6.3.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: backend/requirements/*.txt
      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: "24"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: |
            desktop/package-lock.json
            frontend/package-lock.json
            sidecar/package-lock.json
      - run: python -m pip install --upgrade pip==26.1.2
      - run: python -m pip install -r backend/requirements/dev.txt
      - run: npm ci --prefix frontend
      - run: npm ci --prefix sidecar
      - run: npm ci --prefix desktop
      - run: YINSHI_TEST_PYTHON="$(command -v python)" npm test --prefix desktop
      - run: npm run typecheck --prefix desktop
      - run: npm run build:frontend --prefix desktop
      - run: npm run build:helper --prefix desktop
      - run: npm run build --prefix desktop
      - run: file backend/dist/yinshi-desktop-helper | grep -q "Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64"

  sidecar:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: sidecar
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@9c091bb21b7c1c1d1991bb908d89e4e9dddfe3e0 # v7.0.0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@48b55a011bda9f5d6aeb4c2d9c7362e8dae4041e # v6.4.0
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: sidecar/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
      - run: node --test tests/*.test.js
      - run: npm audit
      - run: docker build --tag yinshi-sidecar:${{ github.sha }} .

## Repository Conventions

description: Applies implementation and review standards for completeness, validation, control flow, naming, comments, error handling, state, explicit options, and testing. Use before writing, modifying, refactoring, or reviewing code in any language.

# Coding Practices

Follow more specific repository conventions when they differ. Apply every relevant rule below.

## Completeness

Deliver complete behavior at the repository's quality bar. A release may omit features, but existing behavior must be sound. Do not leave TODOs, placeholder implementations, or temporary shortcuts. If work cannot be completed now, open an issue instead of leaving an unactionable comment.

## Assertions and Defensive Checks

Validate data at function boundaries. Use assertions for programmer errors and explicit exceptions for user or external input.

Pair checks across related paths. Validate data before writing it to a store and validate it again after reading it back. Check both what must be true and what must not be true, especially at valid-invalid boundaries.

Aim for at least two assertions or defensive checks in each behavior-bearing function. A function without checks should only wire calls together or delegate work.

## Control Flow

Use direct control flow and extract helpers before nesting becomes difficult to follow. Split compound conditions when each branch needs to be independently clear.

Consider whether an `else` should document the unhandled path. State invariants positively, such as `index < length`, rather than through negated boundary checks. Keep function bodies near 50 lines; longer functions usually contain more than one responsibility.

## Naming

Choose exact nouns and verbs that give the reader the correct mental model. Do not abbreviate names when the full term is clearer. Prefer names such as `source`, `target`, and `message_count` over `src`, `dst`, and `msg_cnt`.

Place units and qualifiers after the main noun, such as `latency_ms_max`, so related names sort together. Prefer paired names with similar length, and do not reuse one term for different meanings across subsystems.

## Comments and Documentation

Comments should explain why a choice exists so a reader can judge the tradeoff. Put a short description at the top of each test file that states the covered behavior and how the tests check it. Write comments as complete sentences; brief inline labels are acceptable.

## Error Handling

Handle every signaled error. Do not use a bare catch. Catch a broad exception only when the handler logs and re-raises, translates it into a meaningful domain error, or completely handles the failure. Trace each failure path, and make every caller deal explicitly with failures it can receive.

## Scope and State

Keep state small and local. Declare variables close to first use. Do not duplicate state that can drift from its source. Keep few variables alive at once so misuse remains easy to detect.

## Explicit Options

Spell out options at call sites when defaults affect behavior. Be explicit about encoding, timeouts, sort order, and other settings whose defaults could change or hide intent.

## Testing

The usual stack is Python backends with static HTML and JSON or YAML configuration, but repository conventions control. When adding functionality, update coupled test expectations such as tool or test counts. Run the full test suite after code changes.
